root_cause.text: The MMC core stored `claimed`, `can_retune`, `retune_now`, and `retune_paused` as packed bitfields in the same word, so concurrent read-modify-write updates in `__mmc_claim_host()` and `mmc_mq_queue_rq()` could clobber unrelated flags and leave `host->claimed` falsely cleared, causing spurious `WARN_ON(!host->claimed)`.
root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `claimed` and the retune control flags out of the shared bitfield group into separate `bool` fields, and the commit message explicitly says the “host->claimed bit shared a word with retune flags” and that writes in `__mmc_claim_host()` or `retune_now` updates “can overwrite other bits when concurrent updates happen in other contexts.”

unsigned int		can_retune:1;	/* re-tuning can be used */
unsigned int		retune_now:1;	/* do re-tuning at next req */
unsigned int		retune_paused:1; /* re-tuning is temporarily disabled */

intent_record.what: The `claimed` field in `struct mmc_host` was changed from a 1-bit unsigned bitfield to a standalone `bool`, and the bitfield declarations for `can_retune`, `retune_now`, and `retune_paused` were removed from this excerpt while the surrounding bitfields were left in place.
intent_record.how: At runtime, `claimed` will now occupy a full boolean field instead of sharing a bitfield slot, which changes the struct layout and alignment but not the logical meaning of the flag. The removed bitfield declarations indicate these members are no longer represented in this bitfield group, affecting how the host state is stored and accessed.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add mmc host state flags to track retuning capability and control retuning scheduling and pause behavior.
intent_record.what: Three new boolean fields were added to struct mmc_host: can_retune, retune_now, and retune_paused, each with comments describing retuning capability, deferred retuning, and temporary retuning disablement. These fields were inserted before the existing need_retune and hold_retune members.
intent_record.how: This extends the mmc_host state to track whether retuning is supported, whether it should be performed on the next request, and whether retuning is temporarily paused. At runtime, later code can use these flags to control when tuning operations are allowed or deferred.
